stories.title: Nvidia's Founder Is Out, and the AI Order Shifts
stories.story:
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran it for 33 years, turning a graphics-chip company into the indispensable backbone of the global AI boom. That run ended Thursday when Nvidia's board forced him out, effective immediately, after a cascade of personal and national-security scandals that proved too heavy even for a man who had become the most powerful individual in the AI supply chain.

The trigger was an affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based technology executive at Megaspeed International — Nvidia's primary Southeast Asian distribution partner. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to cultivate Jensen Huang as an intelligence asset. A New York Times investigation then revealed a second affair, this one with a direct Nvidia subordinate. The board, which had already hired an outside law firm to investigate, met Wednesday night and accepted his resignation within hours. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO.

The financial damage was immediate: shares fell more than 10 percent, erasing roughly $1.6 trillion in market value at the worst point. But the structural damage may prove larger. Huang was not merely a CEO; he was Nvidia's chief lobbyist for loosening chip-export controls to China and the architect of a financing ecosystem in which Nvidia quietly backed the smaller cloud companies that, in turn, bought its GPUs. With him gone, venture investors are already signaling that era of Nvidia-underwritten AI financing is likely over. Congressional Democrats have opened an inquiry into whether the relationship with Alice Huang shaped U.S. chip-export policy. The Justice Department is separately probing whether Megaspeed-linked entities diverted advanced AI hardware to China — hardware that researchers have already traced, through weight analysis, to Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips running inside Chinese frontier models.

The implied next chapter is tighter export controls, harder boardroom scrutiny of founder-CEOs in dual-use industries, and an AMD that suddenly has an opening it has not had since 2022.
stories.hook: The man who built the engine of the AI race was apparently also the reason Beijing had a seat at the wheel.
stories.source: Al Jazeera, U.S. News & World Report, CNBC, Wikipedia (Jensen Huang spying scandal)

stories.title: SpaceX Bets $74 Billion on Becoming AI's Landlord
stories.story:
SpaceX announced plans to invest more than $74 billion in two AI supercomputing campuses — roughly $24 billion at its Starbase rocket site in South Texas and $50 billion in Cochise County, Arizona — a figure that rivals the GDP of a mid-sized country and dwarfs any single data center commitment in history.

The logic is straightforward once you see the revenue line. SpaceX's AI segment, operating under the xAI subsidiary it absorbed earlier this year, generated more than half of the company's total revenue in the third quarter alone — more than rockets, more than Starlink. Anthropic already pays $1.25 billion a month to rent compute at the Memphis Colossus cluster; Google pays $920 million monthly for a similar arrangement. SpaceX is now betting it can replicate that landlord model at a scale no competitor can match.

The timing is charged. The Nvidia leadership vacuum announced yesterday removes the industry's most effective advocate for loosening chip export controls. That vacuum creates both risk and opportunity for SpaceX: riskier access to Blackwell GPUs for new builds, but a weaker lobby opposing the kind of vertically integrated compute empire Musk is assembling. The Texas campus plans even include a private gas-fired power plant, insulating the facility from grid constraints that have hobbled rivals.

Local resistance is real. A petition against the Arizona campus has 2,400 signatures, and Texas's incoming governor campaigned explicitly on a moratorium on new data centers. The Cochise County commission must still approve the $50 billion Arizona site. These are not trivial hurdles — but they are the kinds of hurdles that $74 billion has a way of clearing.
stories.hook: When a rocket company makes more money renting computers than launching satellites, you're watching an industry reorganize in real time.

stories.title: Inflation Won't Quit, and the Fed May Have to Swing Hard
stories.story:
For five straight years the Federal Reserve has been chasing an inflation rate that refuses to fall to 2%. This week it got the data it was dreading. October consumer prices rose 0.4% month-on-month — beating the 0.3% forecast — and core CPI notched a third consecutive reading of 0.3%, implying an annualized underlying pace of roughly 3.7%. The report landed like a verdict.

The mechanism is familiar but the politics have shifted. Shelter costs, food, and energy are all still climbing. The implied annual rate sits around 4%, well above wage growth of roughly 3.1%, meaning most workers are still losing ground in real terms. What changed this week is that a December hike — once seen as optional — now looks inevitable. Markets quickly priced the probability of the Fed holding steady at zero. More striking: the odds of a 50-basis-point move jumped from essentially nothing to above 12% in a single session, after Governor Christopher Waller said publicly, before the release, that he would support a double hike if core hit 0.3% or higher. It did.

The downstream consequences reach everywhere. The 10-year Treasury yield is hovering near 5.1%, the dollar has hit an 18-month high, and gold is sliding. A stronger dollar tightens financial conditions globally — it raises borrowing costs in emerging markets, stresses dollar-denominated debt, and squeezes commodity importers. The Fed's December 9th decision now carries a question the market had stopped asking: not whether to hike, but by how much. And analysts at Bank of America and Nomura are already gaming whether January gets a second consecutive move — something that would have been unthinkable a fortnight ago.
stories.hook: Inflation has been above 2% for five consecutive years, and the Fed just ran out of excuses to wait.
stories.source: Fox Business / The National News / Bank of America Research, November 2026

stories.title: Microsoft Bets on Cerebras as the Nvidia Alternative Firms Up
stories.story:
For years, Nvidia's moat looked unassailable: not just the chips, but the CUDA software ecosystem that every AI developer had already built their workflows on. Challengers came and went. Then, on the same day Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace, Cerebras Systems quietly announced something that changes the arithmetic.

Cerebras signed Microsoft as a cloud customer — joining AWS and Oracle on its client list — and raised its 2026 revenue forecast to $940–$960 million, up sharply from prior guidance. Adjusted cloud and services revenue more than tripled year-over-year to nearly $145 million in Q3. The order backlog stands at roughly $26 billion, and the company says revenue from the Microsoft deal will begin showing up in Q1 2027. Shares surged 17–19% in after-hours trading.

The timing is not coincidental. Cerebras uses a Wafer-Scale Engine — a chip the size of a dinner plate with 900,000 AI cores — purpose-built for inference speed rather than the GPU cluster approach Nvidia sells. It is a narrower tool, but for certain workloads it is faster and doesn't come with Nvidia's supply backlog problem. Microsoft, which is simultaneously building its own in-house AI silicon, is now hedging along multiple axes at once.

What this implies is a structural shift, not a coup. Nvidia still commands over 90% of AI chip sales. But hyperscalers signing rival chip deals is exactly how dominant platform companies eventually get their pricing power clipped. The Microsoft-Cerebras deal is a small wedge — but it arrived on the most disruptive day in Nvidia's history, and the market noticed AMD and Broadcom rallying even as Nvidia fell. The ecosystem is quietly reorganizing.
stories.hook: The day Nvidia lost its founder may also be the day it lost its monopoly on the conversation.
